lesson.title: The State That Flows but Doesn't Spread
lesson.summary: Liquids hold a fixed volume but take the shape of their container because their particles stay close enough for intermolecular forces to keep them together, while still having enough kinetic energy to slide past one another.
lesson.body:
A liquid is the state of matter in which particles remain close together, similar in spacing to a solid, but retain enough kinetic energy to move around and slide past one another rather than staying locked in fixed positions. This is why liquids have a definite volume, since the particles are still held close together by intermolecular forces, but an indefinite shape, since particles are free to flow and rearrange to match whatever container holds them. Pour water into a cup and it takes the shape of the cup; pour the same water into a wide dish and it spreads out to take that shape instead, all while the total volume of water stays the same.

The particle-level picture of a liquid sits directly between a solid and a gas in the tug of war described in states of matter. Kinetic energy in a liquid is higher than in a solid at the same intermolecular force strength, which is why particles can move past one another instead of merely vibrating in place, but it is not high enough to overcome the intermolecular forces entirely, which is why particles still stay close together rather than flying apart to fill all available space the way a gas does. This intermediate position is also why liquids are far less compressible than gases; since the particles are already touching or nearly touching, there is very little empty space left to squeeze out, whereas a gas is mostly empty space between widely separated particles.

The strength of a liquid's intermolecular forces has direct, measurable consequences for its behavior, and comparing common liquids at room temperature illustrates this well. Diethyl ether, held together only by relatively weak dispersion and dipole-dipole forces, evaporates quickly and boils at just 34.6 degrees Celsius. Water, capable of extensive hydrogen bonding, evaporates much more slowly and boils at 100 degrees Celsius, needing far more thermal energy before its molecules have enough kinetic energy to escape each other's attraction entirely and become a gas. This same comparison of intermolecular force strength across liquids also underlies several everyday liquid properties, including how much energy is needed to evaporate a liquid, how strongly its surface resists being broken, and how easily it flows.

Those three properties, evaporation behavior, surface tension, and viscosity, are all direct consequences of how strongly a liquid's particles attract one another, which means they can all be predicted using the same intermolecular force reasoning developed already. A liquid whose particles interact mainly through weak dispersion forces will generally evaporate readily, form a surface that is easy to disturb, and flow easily, while a liquid whose particles interact through strong hydrogen bonding, like water, will generally do the opposite on all three counts. Surface tension and viscosity, covered next, are simply this same reasoning applied to two specific and very visible behaviors of liquids.
